reference.source: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases / Williams Textbook of Endocrinology
clinicalPearls: The mechanistic mirror image of FGF23-mediated phosphate wasting: here FGF23 signalling is deficient, causing phosphate RETENTION and hyperphosphataemia
Autosomal recessive, caused by loss-of-function mutations in GALNT3 or FGF23 (reducing active intact FGF23) or in KL (klotho, the FGF23 co-receptor), all impairing FGF23 action
Presents with progressive calcified, lobulated masses in periarticular soft tissues, especially around the hips, shoulders, and elbows
Biochemistry shows hyperphosphataemia with increased renal tubular phosphate reabsorption and inappropriately normal or high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D; calcium is usually normal
A related overlapping phenotype is the hyperostosis-hyperphosphataemia syndrome with painful diaphyseal bone lesions
GALNT3 normally glycosylates and protects intact FGF23; its loss increases cleavage so that intact bioactive FGF23 is low despite high total FGF23 fragments
Management aims to lower phosphate through dietary phosphate restriction and phosphate-binding agents, with lesion excision for symptomatic masses
reference.pathophysiology: Hyperphosphataemic familial tumoral calcinosis results from deficient FGF23 signalling. Mutations in FGF23 itself, in GALNT3 (whose O-glycosylation normally protects intact FGF23 from proteolysis), or in KL (encoding klotho, the obligate co-receptor for FGF23) all reduce effective FGF23 action at the kidney. Loss of the normal phosphaturic drive increases proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption, producing hyperphosphataemia, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is inappropriately normal or elevated for the phosphate level, raising the calcium-phosphate product. The resulting supersaturation promotes ectopic calcification in periarticular soft tissue, forming the characteristic lobulated calcified masses, and in some patients a hyperostotic diaphyseal bone reaction. It is the exact counterpart of the FGF23-excess phosphate-wasting rickets syndromes.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary (dystrophic) tumoral calcinosis from chronic kidney disease and hyperphosphataemia
Calcinosis of connective tissue disease (dermatomyositis, systemic sclerosis)
Synovial or bursal chondromatosis and calcific bursitis
Soft-tissue sarcoma or other calcifying mass
Gout and calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease
additionalInvestigations: Serum phosphate (elevated) with tubular reabsorption of phosphate indices
Intact versus C-terminal FGF23 measurement to reveal excess cleavage in GALNT3/FGF23 disease
Radiographs and cross-sectional imaging of periarticular masses
Renal function to exclude secondary tumoral calcinosis of chronic kidney disease
Sequencing of GALNT3, FGF23, and KL to confirm the genotype
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging or ulcerating calcified masses with secondary infection
Painful diaphyseal bone lesions of the hyperostosis variant
Functional impairment or nerve compression from large periarticular deposits
Vascular or visceral calcification from a persistently high calcium-phosphate product
reference.prognosis: Course is chronic and progressive with recurrent masses, but phosphate-lowering measures and selective surgical excision can control disease; recurrence after excision is common if hyperphosphataemia is not corrected.
pitfalls: Confusing primary HFTC with the far commoner secondary tumoral calcinosis of renal failure
Misinterpreting high total FGF23 as excess activity when intact bioactive FGF23 is actually deficient
Excising masses without addressing hyperphosphataemia, leading to recurrence
Overlooking the hyperostosis-hyperphosphataemia bone variant as infection or malignancy
references: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism
management: Reduce serum phosphate through dietary phosphate restriction combined with non-calcium-based phosphate binders to lower the calcium-phosphate product and limit ectopic calcification
Add a phosphaturic agent such as the carbonic anhydrase inhibitor acetazolamide to promote renal phosphate excretion
Consider agents that suppress 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D synthesis to further reduce intestinal phosphate absorption
Surgically excise symptomatic or disabling periarticular calcified masses, recognising that recurrence is likely if hyperphosphataemia is not corrected
Provide analgesia and physiotherapy for painful masses and, in the hyperostosis-hyperphosphataemia variant, painful diaphyseal bone lesions
Monitor phosphate, calcium and renal function periodically to guide phosphate-lowering therapy and detect recurrence
Offer genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance involving GALNT3, FGF23 or KL
